newsitem.title: USA: Racially charged Chevron pollution case halted.
newsitem.headline: Racially charged Chevron pollution case halted.

text.p: A civil trial over Chevron Corp.'s liability for illnesses among residents of a black Houston neighbourhood built on abandoned oil pits was temporarily halted on Friday over alleged racist comments by the judge in the case, a spokeswoman for the residents said.

The U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals will convene a hearing early next week into Chevron's request that U.S. District Court Judge Kenneth Hoyt step down after he questioned whether an Arthritis Foundation study on lupus rates among blacks should be admitted as evidence "because white people wrote it."
"We think we can reconvene the trial next Wednesday or Thursday. That's all I can say," plaintiffs' attorney Benjamin Hall said of a sealed order issued by the appeals court.

Hoyt is presiding over an ongoing trial into whether sludge left behind in 1920s-era oil pits seeped into city water pipes, causing lupus, cancers and other diseases among hundreds of residents of the Kennedy Heights neighbourhood later built on the site.

The oil pits were operated from 1921 to 1927 by Gulf Oil and the property was sold to a developer planning to build a "Negro" neighbourhood on the site, according to testimony in the case. Chevron assumed liability for the pollution when it acquired Gulf Oil years later.
Attorney John O'Quinn, who represents the Kennedy Heights residents, charged Chevron with "environmental racism" and is seeking an estimated $500 million in damages in the case.

In addition to his comments on the lupus study, Hoyt said during a July 16 hearing race was not a factor in determining whether residents of the suburban Houston neighbourhood were sickened by pollutants left behind in the oil pits.
"It's not because they are black, but because they live in a certain area that white people put them in," he said.
According to transcripts of an earlier hearing, Hoyt also said he believed physical differences among races were a product of their environment.
"Why do you think Chinese people are so short? Because there is so much damn wind over there they need to be short. Why are they so tall in Africa? Because they need to be tall. It's environmental.

"I mean, you don't jump up and get a banana off a tree if you're only four feet. If you're seven feet tall and you're standing in China, then you're going to get blown away by that Siberian wind, aren't you?"
Chevron in its initial motion said Hoyt's personal views on race have prevented the company from getting a fair trial.
